description: One short lesson per study topic (data/topics.json). Every fact lists the question ids it answers; together the facts and traps of a lesson cover every question of its topic exactly (checked by the app's tests). Text is English with German exam terms in **bold**. 'common_sense' lists the questions whose wrong options are absurd enough to answer without studying (a judgment call, see DECISIONS.md #13); every other question counts as one to memorize. Written 2026-10-05 from the official answers in data/questions_bayern.json.

lessons.hook: Germany wrote its constitution in 1949 so that a dictatorship could never happen again. That is why human dignity comes first, in Article 1.
summary: The constitution is the **Grundgesetz** (Basic Law).
Article 1: human dignity is untouchable (**Menschenwürde**).
Basic rights include freedom of opinion, of faith and conscience, choosing where you live, and the privacy of letters.
Basic rights can't be voted away, not even by a party in the Bundestag.

facts.text: The German constitution is called the **Grundgesetz** (Basic Law), in force since 1949.
**Article 1** guarantees the **inviolability of human dignity** (die Unantastbarkeit der Menschenwürde): 'Die Würde des Menschen ist unantastbar.'
**Freedom of opinion** (Meinungsfreiheit) is a basic right. It is why people may openly criticise the government, and it covers saying your opinion **on the internet**.
**Freedom of faith and conscience** (Glaubens- und Gewissensfreiheit) is guaranteed too.
**Freizügigkeit** = you may choose yourself where you live.
Opening someone else's letter on purpose breaks the **Briefgeheimnis** (privacy of correspondence).
One basic right is only for foreigners: **asylum** (Asyl) for people persecuted for political reasons.
Freedom of opinion has a limit: you may not **publicly spread false claims about a specific person**.
**Press freedom** is a basic right, so a party in the Bundestag **cannot abolish it**.
The Grundgesetz **bans forced labour** (Zwangsarbeit), and the state may not treat citizens unequally (**Ungleichbehandlung**).
Punishments must respect dignity: a **fine** (Geldstrafe) is allowed; beating, torture and the death penalty are not.

traps.text: 'Everyone should have the same amount of money' is **not** in the Grundgesetz. The real principles next to it (dignity, free speech, equality before the law) are.

lessons.hook: Four words describe the whole German system: republic, democracy, federal state, rule of law.
summary: Germany is a **republic** (not a monarchy) and a **democratic and social federal state** (Bundesstaat).
**Volkssouveränität**: all state power comes from the people.
**Rechtsstaat**: everyone, including the state, must obey the law.
Power is split three ways: Legislative, Executive, Judiciary. The press is not one of them.

facts.text: Germany is a **Republik** (republic), so it is **not a monarchy**.
The official formula: Germany is **'ein demokratischer und sozialer Bundesstaat'** (a democratic and social federal state). If the question is just 'Deutschland ist ...', pick **Bundesstaat**.
**Volkssouveränität** means **'Alle Staatsgewalt geht vom Volke aus'**: all state power comes from the people.
**Rechtsstaat** = all residents **and the state itself** must obey the laws.
Not compatible with a Rechtsstaat: people being **arrested by a private police force without reason**.
A democracy has a free press, so **press censorship** (Pressezensur) is **not** a feature of German democracy.
Three powers: **Legislative** (makes laws: Bundestag and Bundesrat), **Executive** (government, administration, police) and **Judikative** (the courts).
The **press** is sometimes called the 'fourth power', but it is **not a state power**. '**Direktive**' is not a power at all.

traps.text: 'Was gehört **nicht** zur Exekutive?' The answer is **the courts**: they are the Judikative.

lessons.hook: The Bundestag meets in the old Reichstag building in Berlin, the one with the glass dome that visitors can walk up.
summary: The national parliament is the **Bundestag**; it passes the laws.
Elected members are **Abgeordnete**; one party's members together are a **Fraktion**.
**Opposition** = everyone not in government; its job is to control the government.
The **Bundesrat** = representatives of the state governments. Through it the Länder help make federal laws.

facts.text: The parliament for all of Germany is the **Bundestag**, seated in **Berlin** (the picture question shows its building).
New laws are passed by **the parliament** (das Parlament).
The Bundestag elects the chancellor and controls the government, but it does **not form the cabinet**.
The **President of the Bundestag** usually comes from the **strongest parliamentary group** (stärkste Fraktion).
Members of parliament elected by the citizens are **Abgeordnete**.
The members of one party together form a **Fraktion** (parliamentary group).
If members switch to another Fraktion, the **government can lose its majority**.
**Opposition** = all members who don't belong to the governing party or parties. Its job: it **controls the government**.
The **Bundesrat** is made of **representatives of the state governments** (Regierungsvertreter der Bundesländer). Through it the Länder take part in federal law-making.
So a change of government in one Land can make governing in Berlin **harder**, if it **changes the majority in the Bundesrat**.

traps.text: Constitutional organs are Bundestag, Bundesrat, Federal President, federal government and the constitutional court. A **Bürgerversammlung** (citizens' assembly) is **not** one.

lessons.hook: Germany has two heads: the chancellor runs the government, the president represents the country. You vote directly for neither of them.
summary: **Chancellor** (Bundeskanzler, now **Friedrich Merz**): elected by the **Bundestag**, leads the cabinet.
**Federal President** (Bundespräsident, now **Frank-Walter Steinmeier**): head of state, represents Germany.
The president is elected by the **Bundesversammlung**, proposes the chancellor and appoints the ministers.

facts.text: The **Bundestag** elects the chancellor.
The chancellor **leads the federal cabinet** (Bundeskabinett).
The chancellor works mostly **in Berlin**, where the Chancellery and the Bundestag are.
The current chancellor is **Friedrich Merz** (since May 2025).
The head of state (Staatsoberhaupt) is the **Bundespräsident**, currently **Frank-Walter Steinmeier**.
The president's main job: **representing the country**.
The president is elected by the **Bundesversammlung** (the Bundestag members plus the same number of delegates from the states), so citizens **can't vote for the president directly**.
The president **proposes the chancellor** for election (the picture: President Heinemann hands Helmut Schmidt his appointment, 1974) and **appoints the ministers**.
Germany's honour for service to the country is the **Bundesverdienstkreuz** (Federal Cross of Merit).
The **Bundeswehr** is the German army.

traps.text: Who appoints the ministers? The **Federal President**, not the presidents of the Bundestag, the Bundesrat or the constitutional court.

lessons.hook: Germany is almost always governed by coalitions, and they get nicknames from the party colours, like the 'Ampel' (traffic light).
summary: **CDU**, **CSU**, **SPD**, **FDP**: know what the letters stand for.
Parties working together to form a government = **Koalition**.
The two biggest groups in today's Bundestag: **CDU/CSU and AfD**.
A party that fights the constitution can be banned.

facts.text: **CDU** = Christlich Demokratische Union. **CSU** = Christlich Soziale Union, the CDU's sister party that only runs in Bayern.
**SPD** = Sozialdemokratische Partei Deutschlands. **FDP** = Freie Demokratische Partei.
The two largest parliamentary groups (Fraktionen) are currently **CDU/CSU and AfD** (since the February 2025 election).
Parties working together to form a government = **Koalition**.
**Ampelkoalition** (traffic light) = **SPD** (red), **FDP** (yellow) and **Bündnis 90/Die Grünen** (green).
Why more than one party? So that **the different opinions of citizens are represented**.
A party aiming for a dictatorship is **verfassungswidrig** (unconstitutional). A party can be banned **when it fights against the constitution**, not for criticising the government.

lessons.hook: German elections run on three words you will see again and again: frei, gleich, geheim.
summary: Elections are **free, equal and secret** (frei, gleich, geheim).
The people elect the **Bundestag**; voters must be **German citizens aged 18+**.
Voting is a **right, not a duty**. 'Aktives Wahlrecht' = you may vote.
The party with the most votes wins; regular elections make a change of government possible.

facts.text: The **eligible people** (das wahlberechtigte Volk) elect the members of the Bundestag. The **Bundestag** is the body the people elect, and the Bundestag election is the election of **the parliament for Germany**.
You may vote in a Bundestag election if you are a **German citizen and at least 18**.
Taking part in elections is **a right** (ein Recht). Nobody has to vote.
**Aktives Wahlrecht** = being allowed **to vote**. (Passives Wahlrecht would be the right to be elected.)
**Frei** (free): nobody may influence or force you, a vote brings you no disadvantage, and you decide **without pressure whether and whom** you vote for.
Elections are **geheim** (secret); the full formula is **frei, gleich, geheim**.
The party that gets **the most votes** wins.
Regular elections let the majority of voters **change the government**.

traps.text: Two questions ask 'Wahlen sind frei. Was bedeutet das?' The answer is always about **no pressure and no influence**, never 'everyone must vote' or 'you may take money for your vote'.

lessons.hook: Your ballot has two crosses, and the second one (Zweitstimme) decides how many seats each party gets.
summary: Bundestag elections: **every 4 years**.
The **Zweitstimme** decides the seats; a party needs **5%** to get in (5%-Hürde).
Before an election you get a **Wahlbenachrichtigung** from your municipality; **Briefwahl** (postal vote) is allowed.
**Wahlhelfer** count the votes. It's an honorary job citizens must accept if asked.

facts.text: The Bundestag is elected for **4 years**, so there are elections **every four years**.
The system mixes **majority and proportional voting** (Mehrheits- und Verhältniswahlrecht): the **Erststimme** goes to a local candidate, the **Zweitstimme** to a party.
The more **Zweitstimmen** a party gets, **the more seats** it gets in parliament.
**5%-Hürde**: a party needs at least **5% of the Zweitstimmen** to enter the Bundestag. It is a minimum share of the votes.
Why? Because **many small parties make forming a government harder**.

Valid = **one cross per column**: one on the left (Erststimme) and one on the right (Zweitstimme). That is **ballot 1**; the others have two or three crosses in one column. Choosing a candidate from one party and the list of another is fine.
Eligible voters get a **Wahlbenachrichtigung** (voting notice) **from their municipality** (Gemeinde).
**Briefwahl** (voting by post) is allowed in Bundestag and Landtag elections.
**Wahlhelfer** (volunteer poll workers) **count the votes** after the polls close. It is the honorary job citizens **must accept** when asked.

lessons.hook: Germany has 16 states with their own governments, and school is their business, not Berlin's.
summary: **16 Bundesländer**, each with **its own government**, usually led by a **Ministerpräsident**.
Three levels: **Bund, Länder, Kommunen**. The lowest is the **Gemeinde**, led by a **Bürgermeister**.
**School policy** is a job of the Länder.
You can take part locally: citizens' initiatives, volunteering.

facts.text: Germany has **16 Bundesländer**. **Elsass-Lothringen** (Alsace-Lorraine) is **not** one of them; it is in France.
Every Land has **its own government**, mostly headed by a **Ministerpräsident**. Electing a Land parliament is a **Landtagswahl**.
**School policy** (Schulpolitik) is decided mainly by **the Länder**.
Germany is divided into **Bund, Länder und Kommunen** (federation, states, municipalities).
The lowest political level is the **Gemeinde** (municipality); its head is the **Bürgermeister**.
The **Ordnungsamt** (public order office) belongs to the municipal administration.
They want to cut your bus line? **Join or start a Bürgerinitiative** (citizens' initiative).
**Ehrenamtlich** = working **voluntarily and unpaid** in clubs and associations (Vereine und Verbände).

lessons.hook: In German courts, ordinary citizens sometimes sit next to the judges, as Schöffen.
summary: The **Bundesverfassungsgericht** interprets the Grundgesetz.
Judges belong to the **Judikative** (rechtsprechende Gewalt); their job is to deliver verdicts.
**Schöffen** are volunteer judges; a **Rechtsanwalt** advises and represents you.
Criminal responsibility starts at **14**.

facts.text: The **Bundesverfassungsgericht** (Federal Constitutional Court, in Karlsruhe) interprets the Grundgesetz.
A court case is a **Prozess**. There is a criminal trial when someone **has committed a crime and is charged**.
A judge **works at a court and delivers verdicts**: **Recht sprechen**.
Judges belong to the **Judikative**, the **rechtsprechende Gewalt** (judicial power).
**Schöffen** are **volunteer judges** (ehrenamtliche Richter) who decide **guilt and punishment** together with the professional judges.
A **Rechtsanwalt** (lawyer) advises on legal questions and represents people in court.
The **police** watch that laws are obeyed.
Young people are **strafmündig from 14**: from that age they **are punished** for crimes.

lessons.hook: If you have a job in Germany, social insurance comes out of your pay automatically. That is how the welfare state is paid for.
summary: The economic system is the **soziale Marktwirtschaft**: a free market, but the state ensures social balance.
Social insurance is paid **automatically**, by **employers and employees together**.
**Life insurance** is not social insurance, and **VAT** is not taken from your salary.

facts.text: The economy is a **soziale Marktwirtschaft**: it follows **supply and demand**, but **the state ensures social balance**.
It is financed by **Sozialabgaben** (social contributions), paid by **employers and employees** together, and **automatically** if you have a permanent job.
It includes **health insurance** (which creates social security), pension, unemployment and **long-term care insurance** (Pflegeversicherung).
The state **builds roads and schools**, pays Kindergeld, supports museums and athletes, but it does **not pay holidays for everyone**.

traps.text: Not part of the statutory social insurance: **life insurance** (Lebensversicherung).
An employee does **not** pay **Umsatzsteuer** (VAT) out of her salary. Wage tax (Lohnsteuer) and social contributions, yes.

lessons.hook: Most answers in this topic hang on four years: 1933, 1938, 1939 and 1945.
summary: The Nazis ruled **1933-1945**; Hitler became chancellor in **1933** and set up a **dictatorship**.
**9 November 1938**: synagogues and Jewish shops were destroyed.
**World War II: 1939-1945**. It ended in Europe on **8 May 1945** with Germany's unconditional surrender.
**Stauffenberg**: the attempt on Hitler's life on **20 July 1944**.

facts.text: The Nazis under Hitler were in power from **1933 to 1945**; Hitler became **Reichskanzler in 1933**.
They built a **dictatorship**: the 'Third Reich' was a **Diktatur**.
There were **no free elections**, parties were **banned**, and the state's policy was **state racism**.
On **9 November 1938**, Nazis and their followers **destroyed Jewish shops and synagogues**.
**World War II** lasted from **1939 to 1945**.
**Claus Schenk Graf von Stauffenberg** is known for the **assassination attempt on Hitler on 20 July 1944**.
The war ended in Europe on **8 May 1945** (the year to remember: **1945**) with Germany's **unconditional surrender**.

traps.text: 'Was gab es **nicht** in der NS-Zeit?' The answer is **free elections**. Press censorship, arbitrary arrests and persecution of Jews all **did** exist.

lessons.hook: Jewish life in Germany is older than Germany: the first documented community, in Cologne, dates from the year 321.
summary: Jewish communities have existed here for **about 1700 years**; the largest today are in **Berlin and Munich**.
Denying the Holocaust is antisemitic and a crime: up to **5 years** in prison or a fine.
Germany's special responsibility for Israel comes from the **Nazi crimes against Jews**.
Remembrance: **27 January**, **Stolpersteine**, Willy Brandt's **Kniefall** (1970).

facts.text: The first Jewish community on today's German territory existed **about 1700 years ago**.
The largest Jewish communities are in **Berlin and Munich**.
The Jewish house of prayer is the **Synagoge**.
The roughly 40 **Makkabi** sports clubs are open to **everyone**.
**Denying the Holocaust** is antisemitic and can be punished with **up to five years in prison or a fine**.
**Publicly calling for the destruction of Israel** is forbidden.
Israel was founded on the basis of a **United Nations resolution**.
Germany's special responsibility for Israel comes from the **Nazi crimes against Jews**.
**Stolpersteine**, small brass plates in the pavement in front of houses, remember **victims of National Socialism** who lived there.
**27 January** (the liberation of Auschwitz in 1945) is the day of remembrance for the **victims of National Socialism**.
**1970, Warsaw**: Chancellor **Willy Brandt** knelt at the ghetto memorial, asking **Poland and the Polish Jews for forgiveness**.

lessons.hook: For almost a year, West Berlin was supplied entirely by air: the 'raisin bombers' landed every few minutes.
summary: After 1945: **4 occupation powers** (USA, UK, France, Soviet Union), **4 zones**, Berlin in **4 sectors**.
1948/49 **Luftbrücke** (airlift): the Soviets had blocked the land routes to West Berlin.
**1949**: the Federal Republic is founded, first chancellor **Konrad Adenauer**. **1950s**: the Wirtschaftswunder.
**Gastarbeiter** came from the 1950s on, the first from **Italy**; most migrants overall came from **Turkey**.

facts.text: The four **Allied occupation powers** were the **USA, the Soviet Union, Great Britain and France**. **Japan** was not one of them.
Germany had **4 occupation zones**. On the map: **1 = Great Britain** (north-west), **2 = Soviet Union** (east), **3 = USA** (south, with Bayern), **4 = France** (south-west).
**Berlin** was divided into **four sectors**.
**Luftbrücke**, June 1948 to May 1949: West Berlin was supplied by air because **the Soviet Union had cut off all land routes**.
The Federal Republic was founded in **1949**; its first chancellor was **Konrad Adenauer**.
The **Wirtschaftswunder** (economic miracle) happened in the **1950s**.
**Willy Brandt** stands for the **Ostverträge** (the treaties with the Eastern bloc).
The '**Iron Curtain**' meant the **Warsaw Pact sealing itself off from the West**.
Foreign workers recruited in the 1950s and 60s were called **Gastarbeiter**; the first came from **Italy**.
Most migrants to Germany came from **Turkey**.
In the **GDR**, migrants came mainly from **Vietnam, Poland and Mozambique**.

lessons.hook: The GDR called itself 'democratic', but it was a one-party dictatorship watched over by the Stasi.
summary: **DDR** = Deutsche Demokratische Republik, **1949-1990**, founded in the **Soviet zone**.
It belonged to the **Warsaw Pact**; its economy was a **Planwirtschaft**.
**Stasi** = Ministerium für Staatssicherheit, the secret service.
**17 June 1953**: strikes and a popular uprising.

facts.text: **DDR** = **Deutsche Demokratische Republik** (GDR), founded in **1949** in the **Soviet occupation zone**; it existed from **1949 to 1990**.
Its flag was **black-red-gold with hammer, compass and a wreath of grain**; its coat of arms is picture **4**.
In the Cold War the GDR belonged to the **Warsaw Pact**, the Eastern military alliance.
Its economy was a **Planwirtschaft** (planned economy).
**Stasi** = **Ministerium für Staatssicherheit**, the GDR's **secret service**.
**17 June 1953**: **nationwide strikes and a popular uprising**. West Germany long marked the day as a public holiday.

lessons.hook: The Wall stood for 28 years: built by the GDR in 1961, opened in 1989.
summary: The **GDR** built the Wall in **1961**; Berlin stayed divided until **1989**.
**1989**: 'Wir sind das Volk' (Monday demonstrations), the **Wende**, the Wall opens.
**3 October 1990**: reunification. **5 eastern states** joined the Federal Republic, under chancellor **Helmut Kohl**.
The 5 eastern states: **Brandenburg, Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, Sachsen, Sachsen-Anhalt, Thüringen**.

facts.text: **The GDR** built the Wall in Berlin in **1961**; from **1961 to 1989** Berlin was **divided by a wall**.
'**Wir sind das Volk**' was the call of the **Monday demonstrations in 1989 in the GDR**.
The **Wende** (autumn 1989): the GDR changed **from a dictatorship to a democracy**.
The Wall was opened for everyone in **1989** (on 9 November).
**Deutsche Wiedervereinigung** (reunification), 1990: **the five eastern states joined the Federal Republic**. It is celebrated on **3 October**, the Tag der Deutschen **Einheit**.
**Helmut Kohl** is called the 'chancellor of German unity'.
Germany has had **today's borders since 1990**, and with reunification the new states also became part of the **EU**.

**Brandenburg, Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, Sachsen, Sachsen-Anhalt, Thüringen**. In every 'which state belonged to the GDR?' question exactly one option is on this list; in the list question, pick the list of exactly these five.

lessons.hook: The EU began as a peace project: former enemies like France and Germany chose to trade instead of fight.
summary: Germany is a **founding member**; the **Treaties of Rome** (1957) created the **EEC (EWG)**.
**27 member states**, euro cash since **2002**, and **Schengen** means no passport checks.
The European Parliament is elected **every 5 years** and works in **Strasbourg, Luxembourg and Brussels**.

facts.text: Germany is a **founding member** of the EU.
The **Treaties of Rome** (1957, celebrated 50 years later in 2007) founded the **European Economic Community (EWG)**.
The goal shown by Mitterrand and Kohl at Verdun (picture question): **peace and security** in the EU.
**Europäische Integration** = European states **joining together in the EU**.
**EU** = **Europäische Union**, with **27 member states**. Its flag is the **circle of yellow stars on blue** (picture **2**).
**Schengen**: Germans can travel to many European countries **without passport control**.
People in Germany have paid **in cash with euros since 2002**.
It is elected **every 5 years**; in the European election you elect **the members of the European Parliament**.
It works in **Strasbourg, Luxembourg and Brussels**. When asked for one seat, the answer is **Strasbourg** (Straßburg).

lessons.hook: Germany has 9 neighbours. Learn the list once and five questions are free.
summary: The national symbol is the **eagle**: coat of arms picture **1**, and the Bundesadler in the Bundestag.
Flag: **black-red-gold**. Anthem starts: '**Einigkeit und Recht und Freiheit**'.
**Bundesrepublik Deutschland**: about **84 million** people, **9 neighbours**.

facts.text: The coat of arms is the black **eagle** (picture **1**). The **Bundesadler** also hangs in the Bundestag's plenary hall.
The flag is **schwarz-rot-gold** (black-red-gold).
The anthem begins '**Einigkeit und Recht und Freiheit**' (unity and justice and freedom).
Full name: **Bundesrepublik Deutschland**. Population: about **84 million**.

The **9 neighbours**: Denmark (Dänemark), Poland (Polen), Czech Republic (Tschechien), Austria (Österreich), Switzerland (Schweiz), France, Luxembourg, Belgium, Netherlands. In each 'Nachbarland' question exactly one option is on this list.
**Austria** (Österreich) has a large German-speaking population.

traps.text: In the Bundestag hangs the **Bundesadler** (federal eagle). The option **Reichsadler** (the old empire's eagle) is wrong.

lessons.hook: German family law in one line: adults decide for themselves, and children are protected, even from their own parents.
summary: One marriage at a time. You marry at the **Standesamt**; a divorce needs a **lawyer** and usually a **separation year**.
**Parents** raise their children, and **hitting a child is punishable**.
Help with bringing up children: the **Jugendamt**, which can even take a child out of a violent family.
Adult at **18**. Pregnant women get **Mutterschutz**; Elterngeld needs an **application**.

facts.text: Adults of any combination may live together as a couple, but **Anne (13) and Tim (25)** may not: she is a child.
You may be married to **only one partner at a time**, so a man married to two women is **not allowed**.
To get married, you go first to the **Standesamt** (registry office).
Divorce usually comes after the **Trennungsjahr** (the spouses **live separately for at least a year**), and you need a **lawyer**.
Bringing up children is mainly the task of **the parents**.
**Hitting a child can be punished.**
Problems with bringing up your children? The **Jugendamt** (youth welfare office) helps. It can **take a child who is beaten or starved out of the family**.
You are an adult (volljährig) at **18**. Parents must **respect the decisions** of their adult daughter, for example about her boyfriend.
The legal protection shortly before and after birth is **Mutterschutz**.
For **Elterngeld** (parental allowance) you **apply at the Elterngeldstelle**.

lessons.hook: School is compulsory in Germany, and home-schooling is not allowed.
summary: **Schulpflicht** and **Anwesenheitspflicht**: children must go to school, and the state oversees schools.
Parents decide on **religious education until the child is 14**, and on **kindergarten** (a place is guaranteed from age 3).
University needs the **Abitur**; adults can get it at an **Abendgymnasium**. **Volkshochschule** = further education.

facts.text: Most children have **Schulpflicht** (compulsory schooling) and must be present at school (**Anwesenheitspflicht**).
The state controls the schools **because the Grundgesetz makes it its task**.
Until the child turns **14**, the parents decide whether it attends **Religionsunterricht** (religious education).
The **parents** decide whether a child goes to kindergarten. From **age 3** every child has the **right to a kindergarten place**.
To study at a university you normally need the **Abitur**. Adults can catch it up at an **Abendgymnasium** (evening school).
The **Volkshochschule** (VHS) is a place for **further education** (Weiterbildung), for everyone.

lessons.hook: Fired unfairly? Germany has a whole court just for work: the Arbeitsgericht.
summary: Most people work for a **company or public authority**.
**Gewerkschaften** (unions) represent employees; inside a company the **Betriebsrat** helps.
Quitting: mind the **Kündigungsfrist**. Unfair dismissal: **Kündigungsschutzklage** at the **Arbeitsgericht**.
Good training gives the best chances, and you keep learning all your life.

facts.text: Most workers are **employed by a company or a public authority** (Firma oder Behörde).
**Gewerkschaften** (unions) represent **employees** (Arbeitnehmer).
Inside a company, the **Betriebsrat** (works council) helps employees with problems with the employer.
If you want to end your job, respect the **Kündigungsfrist** (notice period).
Fired without good reason? Go to the **Arbeitsgericht** (labour court, responsible for conflicts at work) and file a **Kündigungsschutzklage**.
The best chance of a well-paid job: **be well trained** (gut ausgebildet).
Work changes fast, so **adults must keep learning after their training**.
The **BIZ** (Berufsinformationszentrum) of the Federal Employment Agency helps with **finding an apprenticeship** (Lehrstelle).

lessons.hook: The easiest topic: in every discrimination question, the answer is the personal trait the question mentions.
summary: **Gleichbehandlung**: nobody may be disadvantaged, for example because of a disability.
Discrimination = being turned down for **who you are** (mother, wheelchair, skin colour), not for missing skills.

facts.text: **Gleichbehandlung** (equal treatment): **nobody may be disadvantaged**, for example because of a **disability**.
Two friends with dark skin are refused entry to a public pool: their right to **Gleichbehandlung** is violated, not freedom of opinion or of assembly.
A woman may **not** be fired because she is **having a child** and her boss knows it. Being often late or doing private things at work can be reasons.

Turned down only because she is a **mother**, he **uses a wheelchair** or he has **dark skin** = discrimination. Turned down for no experience, weak language skills or high salary wishes = not discrimination.

lessons.hook: Germany separates church and state, and yet the state collects church tax for the churches.
summary: **State and religious communities are separate**. Religious tolerance: everyone may believe what they want.
**Christianity** shaped German and European culture. **Church tax** is why the tax return asks about church membership.
The year: **Advent** (4 weeks before Christmas), the Christmas tree, Easter eggs, **Pfingsten** (Christian), **Rosenmontag** costumes.

facts.text: In Germany **state and religious communities are separate** from each other.
**Religious tolerance**: **everyone can believe what they want**.
**Christianity** shaped European and German culture.
Your tax return asks whether you belong to a church **because there is a church tax**, linked to income tax and wage tax.
**Advent** (Adventszeit) = the **last four weeks before Christmas**. At Christmas people **decorate a fir tree** (Tannenbaum).
At Easter people **paint eggs**. **Pfingsten** (Pentecost) is a **Christian holiday**.
Colourful **costumes and masks**: **Rosenmontag** (carnival).

lessons.hook: Most everyday questions follow one pattern: use the official channel. Register, object, complain.
summary: Moving? Register at the **Einwohnermeldeamt**. Night-time quiet starts at **22:00**; the **Hausordnung** has rules for all residents.
Wrong tax assessment: **Einspruch**. Wrong bill from an authority: **Widerspruch**. Treated badly: complain to the **head of the authority**.
Broken new TV: **reklamieren**. Demonstration: **register it**. Restaurant: **Gaststättenerlaubnis**.

facts.text: When you move, you register at the **Einwohnermeldeamt** (residents' registration office).
The legal night-time quiet (**Nachtruhe**) starts at **22:00**. The **Hausordnung** contains **rules all residents must follow**.
Wrong **tax assessment** (Steuerbescheid): **Einspruch einlegen**. Wrong **bill from an authority**: **Widerspruch** with the authority.
Treated badly by an official? You can **complain to the head of the authority** (Behördenleiter).
To open a restaurant you need a **Gaststättenerlaubnis** (restaurant licence) from the responsible authority.
A demonstration in the street **must be registered** (anmelden).
Your new TV doesn't work? **Reklamieren**: take it back to the shop as defective.
Driving licence: the **theory test can be taken in many languages** (more than ten).

lessons.hook: Bayern is the largest German state by area, and officially a 'Freistaat' (free state). Each of these 10 questions is three times as likely to be on your sheet as a general one.
summary: Capital **München**; flag **white-blue**; coat of arms with **white and blue diamonds** (picture 2).
Head of government: **Ministerpräsident**. The Landtag is elected for **5 years**; local elections from **18**.
Bayern has **no foreign minister**: foreign policy belongs to the federal government.

facts.text: Coat of arms: picture **2**, the shield with the **diamond pattern** (Rauten) under a crown. The exam picture is black and white, so look for the shape, not the colours.
The flag is **weiß-blau** (white-blue).
On the map, Bayern is **4**: the **big state in the south-east**.
The capital is **München**. **Altötting** is a Bavarian Landkreis (district).
The head of government is the **Ministerpräsident**, as in most Länder.
The **Landtag** is elected for **5 years** (the Bundestag: 4).
In local elections (Kommunalwahlen) you can vote from **18** in Bayern.
Bayern has ministers for justice, finance and the interior, but **no foreign minister** (Außenminister).
For information on political topics: the **Landeszentrale für politische Bildung**.
